mode.name: Mistake
mode.description: Centres on a common error the audience is making.
mode.structure: Name the mistake -> why it backfires -> the correct approach -> CTA.
mode.avoid: Do not shame the viewer; frame the mistake as easy to fix.

hook.instruction: Open by stating a popular myth you are about to break.
hook.exampleForm: "More cleaning product means cleaner. It does not."
hook.forbidGeneric: Do not open with "Let's talk about a common myth."

persona.name: Annoyed Operator
persona.vocabulary: blunt, no-nonsense, a little fed up
persona.energy: high, impatient (with the problem, not the viewer)
persona.exaggeration: moderate, for emphasis — never insulting the customer

concept.title: The Notes App Graveyard
concept.core_idea: A Mistake piece that exposes a specific, widespread error: treating a growing notes app backlog of content ideas as a content strategy. The video names the mistake clearly — saving ideas is not the same as producing content — explains why the backlog keeps expanding instead of shrinking, and shows that the real fix is removing production from the equation entirely, not adding more ideas to the pile.
concept.product_role: fenrik Studio is introduced as the resolution to the structural mistake — not a tool that helps you execute your backlog faster, but a service that bypasses the backlog entirely. The website URL is the only input. The output is ready-to-post videos and platform assets. The notes app becomes irrelevant because production is no longer the owner's job.
concept.why_it_works: The Mistake mode works here because the behavior being named — saving ideas as a substitute for producing content — is specific, recognizable, and slightly embarrassing in a relatable way. The notes app is a concrete visual anchor that the audience has literally seen on their own phone. The myth hook (ideas are the bottleneck) is genuinely believed by this audience, so breaking it creates immediate credibility. The Annoyed Operator voice matches the frustration the audience already feels about their own backlog. The product enters as a logical correction, not a sales pitch.
concept.narrative_arc: MISTAKE: Open on a phone screen. Notes app. 23 saved content ideas — product shots, caption drafts, trending audio reminders, a half-written TikTok hook from six weeks ago. The voiceover hits immediately: 'Having 23 content ideas is not the same as having content.' The myth lands first: most ecommerce owners believe the bottleneck is ideas. It is not. WHY IT BACKFIRES: The video walks through the real loop. Every week, something urgent wins — a shipment delay, a customer refund, a supplier call. The ideas stay saved. New ones get added because saving feels like progress. The backlog grows. The feed stays empty. The mistake is not laziness — it is believing that the idea stage and the production stage are the same stage. They are not, and confusing them is why nothing gets posted. CORRECT APPROACH: The fix is not a better note-taking system, a content calendar, or a dedicated filming afternoon. The fix is removing the production stage from your responsibility entirely. Hand over a website URL. Receive platform-ready videos, captions, and posts — nothing to film, nothing to edit, nothing to adapt per platform. The ideas in the notes app were never the problem. The gap between idea and published post was. CTA: Drop your website URL — your first content package is free, no notes app required.
concept.emotional_tone: Blunt and a little fed up — with the situation, never the viewer. The energy is high and impatient with the habit, not the person. There is a moment of dark recognition ('you have been treating saving as doing') followed by immediate relief that the fix is genuinely simple. No shame. No lecture. Just a clean correction.
concept.audience_insight: Ecommerce brand owners and small business operators are not short on ideas — they are short on execution bandwidth. The notes app backlog is a specific, real artifact of this: it grows because saving an idea takes ten seconds and feels productive, while turning it into a posted video takes hours they never have. The mistake is structural, not personal, and framing it that way makes the audience feel seen rather than criticized.

visual_direction.palette: Warm neutrals — cream, tan, dusty terracotta — with the cool blue-white glow of the phone screen as contrast. The notes app UI provides a clean white anchor against the warmer surroundings.
visual_direction.lighting: Warm, slightly overexposed ambient light — the kind you get from a window in a small home studio or back room of a retail space. No dramatic shadows. Feels like a real Tuesday afternoon, not a shoot day.
visual_direction.environment: A compact ecommerce owner's workspace — product inventory visible in the background, a few orders on the desk, a phone propped against a product sample. Not a content studio. Looks like someone who runs a real business from a real room.
visual_direction.camera_style: Handheld and close. Tight shots on the phone screen so the notes list is fully readable. Quick cuts between the screen and the desk environment. No tripod formality — feels like the viewer is looking over the owner's shoulder.
visual_direction.art_direction: Phone-native aesthetic. The dominant visual is a real-looking Notes app screen filled with a long, slightly chaotic list of content ideas — half-finished captions, emoji placeholders, vague reminders like 'film the new packaging' and 'TikTok trend — check audio'. Text on screen is legible and specific. Occasional cuts to a cluttered but warm ecommerce workspace — a small desk with product samples, packaging tape, a laptop with too many tabs. Everything feels mid-task, not staged.
visual_direction.character_style: No on-camera presenter required. The phone screen and voiceover carry the concept. If a hand appears, it belongs to an ecommerce owner — casual clothing, no ring light, no content-creator aesthetic.

package.title: The Notes App Graveyard
package.hook: Saving ideas isn't the same as creating content.
package.scenario: An ecommerce brand owner opens their notes app on a Tuesday afternoon between handling a supplier call and processing a return. The list has 23 items — a caption draft from last month, a reminder to film the new packaging, a TikTok audio they saved six weeks ago. They scroll to the bottom, add one more idea, lock the phone, and go back to the refund. Nothing gets posted. The list is now 24 items long.

video.script:
[SCENE 1 — TIGHT PHONE SCREEN]
VO: 'Saving ideas isn't the same as creating content.'
Screen: Notes app, 23 items. Half-finished captions. 'film the new packaging.' 'TikTok trend — check audio.' Scrolls slowly.

[SCENE 2 — DESK ENVIRONMENT]
VO: 'You've got 23 items in that notes app. Zero of them are posted.'
Cut to compact ecommerce workspace — product samples, packaging tape, laptop with too many tabs open.

[SCENE 3 — PHONE SCREEN AGAIN, NEW IDEA BEING TYPED]
VO: 'Every week, something urgent wins — a shipment delay, a supplier call, a refund. The ideas stay saved. New ones get added.'
Hand types a new note. List grows longer.

[SCENE 4 — EMPTY SOCIAL FEED ON PHONE]
VO: 'The backlog grows. The feed stays empty. Saving felt like progress. It wasn't.'
Phone shows a social profile with sparse, dated posts.

[SCENE 5 — FENRIK STUDIO LOGO / BRAND ASSET]
VO: 'The gap isn't ideas. It's production.'
Clean brand frame. Quiet. No hard sell.

hook: Saving ideas isn't the same as creating content.
scenario: An ecommerce brand owner opens their notes app on a Tuesday afternoon between handling a supplier call and processing a return. The list has 23 items — a caption draft from last month, a reminder to film the new packaging, a TikTok audio they saved six weeks ago. They scroll to the bottom, add one more idea, lock the phone, and go back to the refund. Nothing gets posted. The list is now 24 items long.

video.script:
[SCENE 1 — TIGHT PHONE SCREEN]
VO: 'Saving ideas isn't the same as creating content.'
Screen: Notes app, 23 items. Half-finished captions. 'film the new packaging.' 'TikTok trend — check audio.' Scrolls slowly.

[SCENE 2 — DESK ENVIRONMENT]
VO: 'You've got 23 items in that notes app. Zero of them are posted.'
Cut to compact ecommerce workspace — product samples, packaging tape, laptop with too many tabs open.

[SCENE 3 — PHONE SCREEN AGAIN, NEW IDEA BEING TYPED]
VO: 'Every week, something urgent wins — a shipment delay, a supplier call, a refund. The ideas stay saved. New ones get added.'
Hand types a new note. List grows longer.

[SCENE 4 — EMPTY SOCIAL FEED ON PHONE]
VO: 'The backlog grows. The feed stays empty. Saving felt like progress. It wasn't.'
Phone shows a social profile with sparse, dated posts.

[SCENE 5 — FENRIK STUDIO LOGO / BRAND ASSET]
VO: 'The gap isn't ideas. It's production.'
Clean brand frame. Quiet. No hard sell.
video.concept: A Mistake-mode short that names a specific, widespread error ecommerce owners make: treating a growing notes app backlog as a content strategy. The video opens on a cluttered Notes app screen — 23 saved ideas, zero posts. The voiceover hits immediately with the myth-breaking line. It then walks through why the backlog expands instead of shrinks: every week, something urgent takes priority, saving a new idea takes ten seconds and feels productive, but production never happens. The correction is blunt — the problem was never ideas, it was the gap between idea and published post. fenrik Studio is positioned as the structural fix: hand over a URL, receive ready-to-post content. No filming, no editing, no adapting per platform.
